newsitem.title: POLAND: WALESA TO CAMPAIGN FOR SOLIDARITY BLOC BEFORE POLLS.
newsitem.headline: WALESA TO CAMPAIGN FOR SOLIDARITY BLOC BEFORE POLLS.

text.p: Poland's former president Lech Walesa on Monday vowed to throw his weight behind the opposition Solidarity alliance during a run-up to this year's general elections, the Solidarity's leader said.

The leader Marian Krzaklewski said that Walesa, who had remained a political back-bencher since he lost elections in 1995, would actively campaign for the Solidarity Electoral Action (AWS) -- a bloc of more than 30 right-wing parties led by the Solidarity trade union.

"Walesa said that his participation in our electoral campaign must be organised in such a way as to make it the most effective," the leader, Marian Krzaklewski, told a news conference after a meeting with the former president.
Public opinion polls have shown that the Solidarity block may defeat the co-ruling ex-communists in elections due around September.

The polls have given the Solidarity bloc and the ex-communist Democratic Left Alliance a support of between 20 and 29 percent and analysts say smaller parties are likely to hold the balance of power in the next parliament.
Analysts said that Walesa, Solidarity's founder 17 years ago and Poland's president in 1990-1995, may help Solidarity beat the ex-communists by attracting new electorates.
"A person of his authority, if properly used, will definitely be helpful for the Solidarity," said Halina Franczak, a sociologist at the private Demoskop polling institute.
For many Poles Walesa, the 1983 Peace Nobel Prize Laureate, remains a symbol of struggle for the independent Poland during nearly 50 year of communism, which ended in 1989.

Despite his often quarrelsome attitude, which was in part responsible for his defeat in presidential elections in 1995 to ex-communist Aleksander Kwasniewski, Walesa is still popular among many older people, farmers and small towns residents.
Poland's May 25 nationwide referendum on the new constitution, endorsed by the ex-communists and despised by the Solidarity for its secular tone, is seen as a test of strength before the elections.
The Solidarity's electoral bid is widely expected to receive a boost from Polish-born Pope John Paul II, who starts a 10-day visit on May 31.
The Solidarity bloc plans to put up posters with its logo and the Pope across the country before the visit.
